newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Palestinian says talks with Israel deadlocked.
newsitem.headline: Palestinian says talks with Israel deadlocked.

text.p: A Palestinian official said on Tuesday Israel's demand for changes in an agreement on the withdrawal from Hebron in the West Bank had deadlocked peace talks.
The official, who is involved in the negotiations, said a U.S. mediator was expected to propose new ideas to bridge the gap between the two sides when the talks resume on Wednesday.
"We are still in a deadlock. The Americans are expected to come up with bridging proposals," the official, who refused to be named, told Reuters.

Earlier on Tuesday, Palestinian President Yasser Arafat made his first public visit to Israel to underline a renewed Israeli-Palestinian commitment to settle disputes through negotiation instead of violence.

Although the former guerrilla leader expressed disappointment with Israel's approach to the latest peace talks before leaving Gaza by helicopter, he was smiling broadly when met on arrival in Caesarea by Israeli President Ezer Weizman.

The Israel-PLO talks were renewed on Sunday after violence sparked by Netanyahu's opening of an archaeological tunnel near Islamic sites in Arab East Jerusalem last month cost the lives of 59 Palestinians and 15 Israelis.
The PLO official said Israel wanted to reduce the size of a Palestinian police force due to take control of parts of Hebron and was insisting they be armed with pistols and not rifles.
Israel agreed in a deal with the PLO last year to withdraw from most of Hebron after pulling out of other large West Bank towns to make room for Palestinian self-rule.

The redeployment in Hebron, due seven months ago, was postponed after a wave of suicide bombings killed 59 people in the Jewish state. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who ousted Nobel Peace Prize laureate Shimon Peres in elections last May, wants added measures to ensure the security of 400 Jewish settlers in the town holy to Moslems and Jews before pulling his troops back.
But Netanyahu vowed on Sunday during a visit to Israel by U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher that the measures he sought were "within the confines of the existing agreement".
A clause in the Israeli-Palestinian interim agreement signed a year ago says:

"Palestinian police stations or posts will be established in Area H-1 (the area to be handed over to the PLO), manned by a total of up to 400 policemen, equipped with 20 vehicles and armed with 200 pistols and 100 rifles for the protection of those stations."

The Palestinian official said the PLO refused to reopen the agreement but had proposed setting up a joint operation room in Hebron to deal with security issues. He said Israeli negotiators refused to put their proposals in writing.
Israeli security sources said on Sunday the Jewish state was also seeking control over hills in Hebron which the agreement promises to the Palestinians.
Weizman, whose role is largely ceremonial, had announced plans two months ago to invite Arafat when Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was still refusing to see the Palestinian leader.
But the meeting, which was only scheduled on Monday, was timed to coincide with the resumption of peace talks after an emergency summit in Washington last week.
"We are determined to continue with this road of a new Middle East that will be devoid of wars, violence and counter-violence," Arafat said.
"Negotiations will be the tool to resolve our differences," Arafat said after a 25-minute meeting with Weizman, a former defence minister who became an advocate of peace with the Arabs.
Hours after the meeting Israel announced it would let 10,000 Palestinians enter the Jewish state from the Gaza Strip for work beginning on Wednesday, easing a two-week closure on the area.
